# PHP newline not working in text file

You are encountering this issue because you are treating `\n` as a literal string rather than a control character. In your code snippet, `$number . '\n'` concatenates the variable content with the two-character sequence backslash and n. When `fwrite()` writes this to the file, it outputs exactly what was given: the text `\n`.

This is a fundamental misunderstanding of how escape sequences work in PHP strings versus how they behave during I/O operations. To generate an actual newline character (ASCII 10), you must use a double-quoted string or the `chr()` function. In single-quoted strings, backslashes are treated as literal characters unless part of an escape sequence recognized by the language parser, but simply typing `'\\n'` or `'\n'` inside single quotes results in the literal characters `\` and `n`.

```php
// Incorrect: Writes literal "\n" to the file
$numberNewline = $number . '\n'; 

// Correct approach 1: Use double quotes for escape sequence interpretation
$newlineContent = $number . "\n";

// Correct approach 2: Explicitly use chr()
$newlineContent = $number . chr(10);
```

The problem manifests differently depending on your operating system's line ending conventions. You mentioned running this on a Mac. Historically, macOS used `\r` (carriage return) as the line ending, while Windows uses `\r\n`, and modern Unix-like systems use only `\n`. However, PHP handles string escaping based on the source code syntax, not the runtime OS environment.

If you intend to write standard Unix-style newlines, using `"\n"` is the correct approach for cross-platform compatibility in most contexts. If you are running on macOS and specifically need to match legacy Mac file formats, you might consider `\r`, but this is rarely necessary for modern development workflows. The real culprit here is almost certainly the single quotes used in your concatenation logic.

When debugging `fwrite` issues, always verify what data actually lands on disk using a hex dump. This reveals whether the file contains ASCII 10 (the newline) or the literal characters 92 and 110 (backslash and n). You can do this with standard Unix tools:

```bash
# View raw bytes including newlines
hexdump -C your_file.txt

# Or use xxd for a cleaner hex view
xxd your_file.txt
```

If you see `5c` followed by `6e` in the hex dump, that confirms the file contains the literal text `\n`. If you see `0a`, the newline worked correctly.

Another common pitfall involves how `fwrite` interacts with different line ending expectations. Some developers assume that `file_put_contents()` or `fwrite()` will automatically convert newlines based on the server's OS configuration. While some functions might handle line endings depending on stream wrappers, relying on implicit conversion is dangerous. Explicitly defining the byte sequence you want ensures portability across Windows, Linux, and macOS servers.

If you are working within a Laravel application or any framework that generates log files, ensure your custom logging methods respect the same newline standards used by the framework's built-in logs. Inconsistent line endings can break diff tools, git history, and parser logic downstream in your pipeline. For robust text processing, always normalize line endings to `\n` regardless of the server environment.

For further reading on file handling best practices in PHP, you might refer to resources like [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com) which often discuss common pitfalls in application maintenance and file I/O strategies.
